notes.title: The definite articles o and a

blocks.text: A noun refers to a person, place or thing. Very few English nouns have a masculine or feminine form — host/hostess is a rare one — but every noun in Portuguese has a grammatical gender. The definite article, the, is o for masculine and a for feminine, and it reflects that gender.
People
Places and things have a gender too
But the ending doesn't always tell you
o and a are used far more often than the is in English, and they always tell you the gender. So when you learn a new noun, learn it with its article — not casa but a casa.
One and two are the numbers that change with gender: they agree with the noun they refer to. You'll meet the rest of the numbers in the next lesson.

blocks.text: The lesson closes with a short monologue in which a speaker introduces her family. Rather than reproduce it here, this is the pattern it drills — every sentence is há plus a family word plus a name, which is exactly what you'd say introducing your own.

rows: I want to introduce my family.
Na minha família há um pai, o Sr. Carlos.
In my family there's a father, Mr. Carlos.
Há uma mãe, a Sra. Ana.
There's a brother, Pedro, a teacher.
E há uma irmã, Sônia, médica.

blocks.text: Words ending in –a, –e, –o, or the consonants –s, –m or –ns are usually stressed on the second-to-last syllable.
Words ending in –i or –u (or –i/–u followed by –m or –s), or in a diphthong, are stressed on the last syllable.

If a word follows neither rule, a written accent marks the stressed syllable. On í and ú the acute simply marks stress; on á, é and ó it marks stress and an open vowel. The circumflex on â, ê and ô marks a closed vowel. The grave accent, used only on à in certain contractions, doesn't change stress at all.
A diphthong is two vowels making one sound together — the ei in seis (six) sounds like the a in hate.
They has a masculine and a feminine form: eles and elas. And Portuguese has no subject pronoun for it.
Ter is irregular. The accent on the second and third person plural doesn't change the pronunciation.
In sentences
Filhos can mean four sons, or sons and daughters together. The same logic applies to friends: nós temos amigas is a group of women, while nós temos amigos is either all men or a mixed group.

blocks.text: In quarto the r is that breathy h, or a flap. Cariocas in Rio famously trill their r more; paulistanos in São Paulo soften it. In small towns it can be longer, close to the American r. These regional differences are rarely strong enough to confuse anyone — and newscasters everywhere speak a standard Brazilian Portuguese, much as they do in the U.S.

Most regular infinitives end in –ar, –er or –ir, and each type follows its own pattern of endings. This lesson takes the –ar verbs, like falar (to speak).
Eu and nós can be dropped — the ending already says who the subject is. Estudo espanhol means I study Spanish; Estudamos matemática, We study math.
In sentences
More –ar verbs
Careful: aprender ends in –er, not –ar, so it doesn't take these endings. The book lists it here among the vocabulary, not as an –ar verb.

blocks.text: A false friend to watch: entrada means appetizer, not entrée. The main course is o prato principal.

You'll meet the verb gostar properly in a later lesson. For ordering, eu gostaria (I'd like) is the courteous form. Eu quero (I want) is more direct. And when someone asks what you'd like, they often say o que você deseja — literally what do you wish.

rows: Que tipo de vinho o senhor deseja?

blocks.text: Words that point: this, that, these, those. They agree in number and gender with the noun — and where English makes two distinctions of distance, Portuguese makes three.
este / esta — near both of you
esse / essa — near the person you're speaking to

rows: Esse guardanapo no chão é seu?
Is that napkin on the floor yours?

blocks.text: aquele / aquela — away from you both

rows: Aqueles jogadores de futebol são ótimos.

blocks.text: When you don't know what the thing is
There are neuter, invariable forms for when you can't tell the gender — or don't know what you're pointing at.

In informal spoken Brazilian Portuguese not much attention is paid to the este/esse distinction. Speaking, you can use esse or isso for this, esses for these, aquele or aquilo for that, and aqueles for those.
Prato does three jobs: prato principal is the main course, prato is a plate, and pratos in the plural also means dishes in general — Lave os pratos! Wash the dishes!

notes.title: Tomar — to take, and to have

blocks.text: Tomar means to take: Tome uma aspirina, take an aspirin. But it also means to have, when what you're having is food or drink.

blocks.text: The days are not capitalized, and feira is optional in speech — segunda, terça, quarta. For something happening on a particular day use no for sábado and domingo, which are masculine, and na for the others, which are feminine.

Quem é o seu cantor predileto?

blocks.text: Gostar is a regular –ar verb, but what it likes is always introduced by de — and that de can be followed by a noun or by another verb.

rows: Eu não gosto de filmes violentos.
Eu não gosto de assistir filmes violentos.
I don't like to watch violent movies.

blocks.text: For something specific, de contracts with the article

rows: Você gosta da amiga da Carol?
Vocês gostam dos planos para as férias?
Do you like the vacation plans?

blocks.text: That is the whole trick: gostar de + something in general, gostar do/da/dos/das + something specific.

notes.title: Three irregular verbs: ler, vir, dar

rows: Nós não lemos o jornal todos os dias.
We don't read the newspaper every day.
O Pedro e a Cecília vêm jantar em casa.
Pedro and Cecilia are coming over for dinner.
A que horas você vem aqui?
What time are you coming here?
Quando vocês dão jantares em casa?
When do you give dinner parties at home?
Você quer ir a uma festa?
Do you want to go to a party?
When do you want to travel?
I can have dinner on Saturday.
Eles não podem vir à inauguração.
They can't come to the opening.
Eu posso ir lá a pé?
Do you want to go out with me?

blocks.text: Sair means to leave, to get out, or to go out — and it does all three.

rows: Que horas sai o trem para Belo Horizonte?
What time does the train to Belo Horizonte leave?
Vocês saem do trabalho às cinco ou às seis da tarde?
Do you leave work at 5 or 6 p.m.?
A Paula e o Pedro saem juntos.
Paula and Pedro go out together.
Aos domingos eu saio com meus amigos.
On Sundays I go out with my friends.
Vamos sair de casa e ir ao cinema!
Let's get out of the house and go to the movies!

blocks.text: Portuguese splits the English word ticket three ways.

rows: for a movie, a concert, a show, a game or a play
for transport — bilhete de avião, passagem de trem, bilhete de ônibus
Nós queremos dois ingressos para a sessão das dezenove horas, por favor.
We want two tickets for the 7:00 p.m. show, please.
Eu gostaria de uma entrada para o show das dezenove e trinta.
I'd like a ticket for the 7:30 p.m. show.
Eu gostaria de uma passagem para o trem das vinte horas para o Rio de Janeiro, por favor.
I'd like a ticket for the 8:00 p.m. train to Rio de Janeiro, please.
O nosso bilhete de avião está na minha bolsa.
Our airplane ticket is in my handbag.

blocks.text: And two words for concert: um concerto is a classical concert, while a pop, rock or samba gig is um show. Jogar is to play a game or a sport; tocar is to play an instrument.
Querer means to want, and like English it is followed by a noun or by a verb in the infinitive.

rows: Eu quero um ingresso para o jogo de tênis.
I want a ticket for the tennis game.
We want to travel by ship.
O que você quer para o café da manhã?
What do you want for breakfast?

blocks.text: Poder means can, or to be able to, and is also followed by an infinitive.
Poder carries both English senses. Ability: eu posso tocar piano, I can play the piano. Possibility: eu posso ir ao cinema amanhã, I can go to the movies tomorrow.

rows: Eles não podem correr a maratona.
Os meus amigos não podem vir no domingo.
My friends can't come on Sunday.
Que horas você pode sair na sexta-feira?
What time can you go out on Friday?

blocks.text: De contracts with the demonstratives too, exactly as it does with the articles.

head: Singular
Plural
rows: de + isto = disto; de + isso = disso
Nós não gostamos daquele novo filme.
We didn't like that new movie.

blocks.text: Two friends talk about films, theatre and what they like doing at the weekend.

rows: Você gosta de filmes de ação?
Às vezes, mas prefiro filmes antigos como Casablanca.
Sometimes, but I prefer old movies like Casablanca.
Que legal! Eu também. Eu amo Humphrey Bogart. Ele é o meu ator favorito!
Cool! Me too. I love Humphrey Bogart. He's my favorite actor!
E teatro? Você vai ao teatro?
And the theater? Do you go to the theater?
Sim vou, mas não muito porque é caro.
Yes, I do, but not a lot because it's expensive.
Concordo, principalmente para estudantes como nós.
I agree, especially for students like us.
Adoro viajar. Mas não gosto de ir à praia aos domingos porque odeio o trânsito.
I love to travel. But I don't like to go to the beach on Sundays because I hate traffic.
Eu prefiro ficar na cidade aos domingos. Eu posso estudar e ler.
I prefer to stay in the city on Sundays. I can study and read.
Vamos ao cinema mais tarde? Podemos assistir a um filme preto e branco.
Let's go to the movies later? We can watch a black and white movie.
